name: Cope's Rule
statement: Lineages tend to evolve toward larger body size over geological time.
meaning: Over long stretches of the fossil record, many animal lineages appear to trend toward larger average body size — descendants tend to be bigger than their ancestors. It is a proposed macroevolutionary generalisation, not a strict law, and it holds in some lineages while failing in others.
mechanism: Several selective advantages have been proposed to bias lineages upward: larger animals are harder to prey on and better at capturing prey, tend to win intraspecific competition and mating, retain heat more efficiently, and can survive resource scarcity. But size carries costs too — greater resource needs, longer generation times that slow adaptation, and physiological limits — so the upward push is a proposed bias, not a universal force.

examples.text: The textbook illustration: from the small Eohippus to the modern Equus over roughly fifty million years. It is also an oversimplification — horse evolution was a branching bush, not a straight-line size march, and included side branches and size decreases.
Many dinosaur clades show size increase over their history and are frequently cited in support of the rule within specific groups, even as the pattern is far from universal across all lineages.

Marine invertebrates broadly expanded in size across the Palaeozoic, but molluscs are a noted counterexample — Jablonski's 1997 study of Cretaceous molluscs specifically found no consistent size increase, questioning the rule.

variants.name: The passive-trend reading
variants.text: Stanley's and Gould's argument that the apparent trend may be a passive diffusion away from a small ancestral size against a lower size boundary — a lineage starting small can only vary upward — rather than an active selective push toward largeness.

variants.name: The island rule
variants.text: Foster's rule, a contrasting ecogeographic pattern in which insular populations trend to gigantism if small or dwarfism if large — a reminder that size evolution is not uniformly upward.

whyItMatters: It is one of the classic named generalisations about the direction of macroevolution, and a useful lens on why so many familiar lineages produced ever-larger forms. Its contested status — real in some clades, absent or reversed in others, possibly a statistical artefact — makes it a standing case study in how to test a macroevolutionary 'rule'.

working.lead: Treat it as a tendency, not a trajectory
working.text: expect size increase in some lineages and not others; do not assume any given lineage must grow over time.

working.lead: Ask whether the trend is active or passive
working.text: before invoking selection for largeness, check whether the pattern could be passive diffusion from a small-size boundary.
the horse-lineage story is a simplification of a branching history; use it to illustrate, not to prove, the rule.

limits: The rule is empirically contested and does not hold universally: many lineages show no size trend or actively shrink. A major critique holds that the apparent trend is a passive statistical artefact — diffusion away from a small ancestral size against a lower boundary — rather than active selection, with Gould calling it a 'psychological artefact'. Dwarfing may also be hidden by preservation and observational biases. The evidence is genuinely mixed, confirmed in some clades and reversed in others.
misreadings: It is not a law that animals always get bigger, and it was not stated as a rule by Cope himself — the name was applied posthumously, and the concept was also advocated by Depéret. The tidy horse example flattens a branching, non-monotonic history, and the whole pattern may partly reflect statistics rather than a drive toward largeness.
origin: Named for the American palaeontologist Edward Drinker Cope (1840–1897), who favoured directional evolutionary trends, though he did not formulate it as a rule; the name is generally attributed to Bernhard Rensch around 1948, and the French palaeontologist Charles Depéret advanced the same idea, hence the 'Cope–Depéret rule'.

sources.text: Cope's rule, Wikipedia. — the generalisation, the proposed advantages, and the contested empirical status.
